characters: Kwaku: a ten-year-old Ghanaian boy with a neat haircut, warm brown eyes, wearing a green-and-yellow striped polo shirt and jeans, holding a small smooth wooden susu savings box.
Papa: Kwaku’s father, a skilled, hard-working carpenter in hislate thirties wearing a denim work apron and holding a carpenter’s pencil.
Maame: Kwaku’s mother, a kind, practical seamstress and homemaker wearing a patterned indigo-and-cream dress.
Ama: Kwaku’s six-year-old little sister with yellow hair ribbons.

notes: Give Papa’s words on page 7 extra warmth and dignity.

music: Optional low-key soft piano ambience (user-togglable in reader header; off by default).
culturalNotes: Honours the Ghanaian susu tradition and models empathy without stigmatising low income.

pages.brief: Warm sunlit carpentry workshop in Kumasi: Papa (denim carpenter apron, kind smile) handing a small polished wooden susu savings box with a slot on top to ten-year-old Kwaku (green-and-yellow striped shirt).
pages.narration: Warm, affectionate father-and-son moment. Clear pronunciation of "Kumasi" and "susu".

pages.brief: At the home table, Maame (indigo-and-cream dress) and Kwaku look at five silver-and-gold one-cedi coins arranged in neat groups beside a notebook.
Close view of Kwaku’s notebook showing simple drawings (no words): a ruler and protractor geometry set on the left side, and a colourful toy top and soda bottle on the right.
Kwaku smiling as he drops three coins into the slot of his wooden susu box, with one coin beside a small envelope and one coin in his hand.
pages.narration: Steady, rhythmic counting of the three parts of the budget: three cedis, one cedi, one cedi.

pages.brief: Sunny afternoon near school: two boys watch a bright plastic spinning top on the ground while Kwaku smiles calmly and steps back without buying.
pages.narration: Lively for the friends, then calm and steady for Kwaku’s choice.

pages.brief: Cosy evening at home with rain outside the window: Maame and Papa sitting together calmly over their household notebook under a warm lamp while Kwaku watches.
Medium close shot: Papa placing a warm, reassuring hand on Kwaku’s shoulder, looking him in the eye with dignity and kindness while Maame smiles supportively.
pages.narration: Warm, dignified, and deeply reassuring. Slow down on "Having less money is never a sign of bad character."

pages.brief: Sunny Saturday morning: Kwaku sitting at the table with his wooden susu box and six neat groups of तीन tally marks in his notebook.
pages.narration: Hopeful and bright as the sun returns and the six weeks are completed.

pages.brief: Kwaku arranging eighteen coins in six neat stacks of three on the wooden table while six-year-old Ama (yellow hair ribbons) claps with delight.
pages.narration: Joyful skip-counting by threes: "Three, six, nine, twelve, fifteen, eighteen cedis!"

pages.brief: Kwaku at his desk holding his new clear plastic geometry set (ruler, compass, protractor) in one hand and dropping three coins back into his wooden susu box with the other.
pages.narration: Proud, warm conclusion. Pause before "The end".

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 4–5 financial literacy and character story set in Kumasi. Teaches needs vs wants, a simple Save-Spend-Share budget, multiplication/subtraction with Ghana cedis, and explicitly affirms the dignity of hard-working families facing external economic challenges.
learningGoals: Distinguish between essential needs and optional wants.
Create a simple Save-Spend-Share budget and calculate savings over multiple weeks.
Explain why financial hardship is caused by real-world circumstances (such as weather, transport or prices) and never measures a person’s worth or character.

subjectLinks.subject: Mathematics (Primary 4–5)
subjectLinks.link: Multiplication, subtraction and budgeting with Ghana cedis.

subjectLinks.subject: Our World Our People / Citizenship
subjectLinks.link: Responsible decision-making, saving (susu), and empathy for others.

subjectLinks.subject: English Language
subjectLinks.link: Fluent reading comprehension, vocabulary and discussion.

beforeReading: Ask: "What is a susu box, and why does having a slot on top help someone save?"
Discuss the difference between something we need for school and something we want for fun.
whileReading: After page 4, verify that Kwaku’s budget adds up to 5 cedis (3 + 1 + 1 = 5).
After page 7, discuss Papa’s words about dignity, hard work, and why we never judge people by their money.
afterReading: Have learners design a pretend 10-cedi weekly budget divided into Save, Spend and Share.
discussion: What helped Kwaku say no to the four-cedi spinning top on Tuesday?
Why was Papa’s message on page 7 so important for Kwaku to hear?
How did keeping 3 cedis in the box after buying the geometry set help Kwaku’s next goal?
reflection: What is one non-money way you can support your family or a friend when times are busy or difficult?

mathsExtension.task: Kwaku saves 3 cedis a week for 6 weeks. How much does he save?
He also puts 1 cedi a week into his sharing envelope for 6 weeks. How much is in the envelope?
Total earned over 6 weeks at 5 cedis per week = ?

support: Count in threes on a number line up to 18 (3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18).
stretch: If Kwaku wants to save 27 cedis for a dictionary at 3 cedis per week, how many weeks will it take? (9 weeks, or 8 weeks if he starts with his 3 leftover cedis!)

culturalNotes: Kwaku (boy born on Wednesday), Kofi (Friday) and Ama (Saturday) are Akan day names; Maame is the Akan address for mother.
Susu boxes (wooden or metal boxes) are a well-known household savings tradition across Ghana.
localiseThis: Check the local price of a school mathematical/geometry set and adjust extension questions if desired.

reviewerNotes: Confirm first syllable vowel (kway vs kwah).
Confirm the vowel in the first syllable (oh vs aw).
Confirm vowel quality and whether the final syllable is stressed.
